title: Exactly solvable model for the diffusive price-dynamics paradox under long-range correlated market-order flow
authors: Yuki Sato, Shunta Fujiwara, Kiyoshi Kanazawa
abstract: We develop an exactly solvable nonlinear time-series model by incorporating the square-root price-impact law into the Lillo--Mike--Farmer (LMF) model to resolve the diffusive price-dynamics paradox under predictable market-order flow. In financial market microstructure, it is well established that the price dynamics are approximately described by Brownian motion at long times. However, it is also well-known that market-order flow is clearly predictable due to long-range correlations, as mathematically formulated by the LMF model. Since market orders have a positive price impact in general, predictable market-order flow seems to contradict Brownian price dynamics. In this work, we resolve this diffusive price-dynamics paradox by developing nonlinear time-series models that generalize the LMF model based on the square-root price-impact law. Our time-series models can be mathematically mapped onto the Lévy-walk framework---an exactly solvable class of non-Markovian stochastic processes developed in statistical physics. We prove that the price dynamics are diffusive at long times under the square-root law even under predictable market-order flow. Our work highlights the crucial practical importance of the square-root law in understanding the microstructural foundation of the Efficient Market Hypothesis.
summary: This theoretical paper resolves a paradox in financial modeling by showing how predictable, correlated market order flow can coexist with diffusive price movements. It achieves this by developing an exactly solvable model that mandates the use of a square-root price impact law. The methodology relies heavily on advanced statistical physics tools like Lévy walks and asymptotic analysis of stochastic processes.
main_problem: The paper resolves the 'diffusive price-dynamics paradox' arising from the contradiction between empirically observed Brownian motion in asset prices and predictable market order flow characterized by long-range correlations.
main_result: By incorporating the square-root price-impact law into an extended Lillo–Mike–Farmer (LMF) model, the authors prove that the price dynamics remain normal diffusive even when the underlying market-order flow exhibits long-range correlation.
method: The approach involves developing and analyzing exactly solvable nonlinear time-series models by mapping them onto the Lévy-walk framework of non-Markovian stochastic processes. Calculations utilize Fourier/Laplace transforms to derive characteristic functions and analyze Mean Squared Displacement (MSD) scaling.
model_or_system: The model is an extension of the LMF framework describing market microstructure, involving $M$ traders whose order flow exhibits long-range correlations ($	ext{LRC}$). The price dynamics are governed by a nonlinear price impact law, assumed to be proportional to the square root of cumulative volume ($I(Q) \propto Q^{1/2}$), which is added to the original state variables.
key_observables: Mean Squared Displacement (MSD) scaling ($\mathbb{E}[(\Delta m(t))^2]$), Order-sign Autocorrelation Function ($	ext{ACF}$), and the characteristic function $P_M(k, t)$.
important_parameters: The correlation exponent $\gamma$ of the order flow, and the price impact exponent $\delta$, with the critical condition being related to $\alpha$ (metaorder distribution exponent) such that $\delta=1/2$ ensures diffusion.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include using the square-root price-impact law ($I(Q) \propto Q^{1/2}$) and assuming specific functional forms for the metaorder-size distribution ($\psi_m(t)$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase diagrams showing the transition between superdiffusion and normal diffusion based on parameters $\alpha$ and $\delta$, with numerical results confirming diffusive behavior under the square-root law.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the paradox, then develops an extended nonlinear time-series model by incorporating the square-root price impact into the LMF framework. The core analysis involves deriving joint probability density functions and characteristic functions using advanced transform techniques to calculate asymptotic scaling laws for MSD.
why_interesting: While applied to finance, the mathematical machinery—analyzing non-Markovian processes (Lévy walks) under long-range memory effects ($	ext{LRC}$) and determining crossover regimes between different diffusion types—is highly relevant to open quantum systems or complex many-body dynamics where correlations decay slowly.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the Lillo–Mike–Farmer model. For each i ∈Ω, the internal state of trader i is characterized by (ϵ(i), R(i), Q(i)), where ϵ(i) is the metaorder sign, R(i) is the remaining metaorder volume, and Q(i) is the cumulative executed metaorder volume. In the coarse-grained description, the market-order sign ϵ(t) is determined by ϵ(t) = ϵ(i(t))(t), where i(t) denotes the ID of the trader submitting the order at time t. Since the metaorder size L obeys a power-law PDF, traders occasionally have large metaorders, which are split into long sequences of child orders. Because all child orders within the same metaorder have the same sign, the market-order sign ϵ(t) exhibits long memory.

FIG. 2. Schematic of the discrete-time LMF price-dynamics model. The system consists of M order-splitting traders. At each time step, one trader is selected with equal probability λ = 1/M and submits a market order. The price is driven by the sum of the traders’ price-impact contributions, according to the additional assumption in Eq. (16).

FIG. 3. Asymptotic behavior of the MSD (23) for the discrete-time LMF price-impact dynamics (19) for the single-trader case M = 1. (a) Phase diagram between superdiffusion (2δ > α) and normal diffusion (2δ < α). The phase boundary is given by 2δ = α. Here, δ ≤1/2 is the necessary and sufficient condition for the MSD to exhibit normal diffusion for any α > 1. (b) Numerical MSD for δ ∈{0.25, 0.5}, α ∈{1.25, 1.5, 1.75}, and M = 1, showing normal diffusion. (c) Numerical MSD for δ ∈{0.75, 1}, α ∈{1.25, 1.5, 1.75}, and M = 1, showing both superdiffusive cases (orange markers) and normally diffusive cases (blue markers). A logarithmic correction appears at the boundary case α = 2δ.

FIG. 4. Numerical results for the price-increment ACF (25) and (34). Panels (a)–(c) correspond to δ = 0.5 and α ∈{1.25, 1.5, 1.75}, with (a) M = 1, (b) M = 5, and (c) M = 10. Panels (d)–(f) correspond to δ = 1.0 and α ∈{1.25, 1.5, 1.75}, with (d) M = 1, (e) M = 5, and (f) M = 10. All results are consistent with our prediction Cr(τ) ∝τ −θ with θ = α −2δ + 1.

FIG. 5. Schematic illustration of the reordering procedure used to derive the exact PDF in the two-body system. In the original time series (left), orders from the two traders are randomly interleaved. By reordering the sample path so that trader 1 submits all orders during t ∈[0, τ1] and trader 2 submits all orders during t ∈[τ1 + 1, t] (right), the price process decomposes into two independent L´evy-walk contributions.
